paper.citation: Alayande KA, Aiyegoro OA, Nengwekhulu TM, Katata-Seru L, Ateba CN. PLoS ONE 15(7): e0235873 (2020)

open_questions.q: Is the deposited GCA_003790365.1 assembly actually contaminated, and if so with what and at what magnitude?
open_questions.basis: NCBI has flagged the assembly with warnings=['contaminated'] and suppressed the RefSeq mirror GCF_003790365.1 on those grounds ('This record was removed by RefSeq staff... Reason: contaminated'). The paper does not mention this. Magnitude is not specified in the record. Because L. reuteri (now Limosilactobacillus) is a piglet-gut isolate, plausible contaminants include co-cultured bulk-gut Firmicutes (Ligilactobacillus, Streptococcus, Enterococcus) or MRS-selective residual host DNA. Without knowing which contigs are foreign, absence claims (esp. C5 no-VF and C4 only-two-AMR-genes) are weaker than the paper implies.
next_steps: Run FCS-GX (NCBI's Foreign Contamination Screen for eukaryotes and cross-taxon Bacteria) against the 420-contig FASTA and enumerate which contigs are flagged and to what putative source taxa.
For each flagged contig, re-check whether any of my abricate hits (esp. plasmid rep30/pLR581, tet(W), lnu(C)) or any of the 31 phage/integrase CDSs sit on it.
Run GTDB-Tk classify_wf on the assembly to see whether the whole thing consensus-classifies as Limosilactobacillus reuteri or whether an appreciable fraction of contigs mis-classify.
Compute average nucleotide identity (fastANI) between the assembly and the L. reuteri type strain DSM 20016 / JCM 1112 --- expect >=95% if the majority is genuinely reuteri.

open_questions.q: Is the frameshifted tet(W) locus phenotypically silent, or does the strain still express tetracycline resistance?
open_questions.basis: All four AMR databases (ResFinder, CARD, NCBI-AMR, ARG-ANNOT) call tet(W) at 100% coverage on contig RJWE01000089.1 --- but PGAP annotates the same locus as pseudo=true with Note=frameshifted (product='tetracycline resistance ribosomal protection protein Tet(W)'). The paper treats it as a presence-based hit and infers a resistance gene without doing a phenotypic MIC. A broken tet(W) ribosomal protection protein would be a null allele. This matters for probiotic safety framing --- a broken tet(W) is safer, and lower risk of horizontal transfer if the ORF is nonfunctional.
next_steps: Perform tetracycline MIC on the live L. reuteri PNW1 isolate by broth microdilution per EUCAST/CLSI, reporting the value against the L. reuteri EFSA/QPS cut-off (8 mg/L).
PCR-amplify the tet(W) locus from PNW1 genomic DNA and Sanger-sequence to confirm the frameshift in the wet strain (not just in the deposited assembly, which may have a sequencing/assembly error).
Check whether the flanking sequence carries conjugation/mobilization machinery (tra genes, oriT, ICE-like modules) that could still enable horizontal transfer of the (broken) tet(W) locus.

open_questions.q: How many, and which type, of prophage regions and CRISPR-Cas arrays are actually present in an improved (long-read) assembly of PNW1?
open_questions.basis: The paper claims 2 intact prophage regions (PHASTER) and 5 CRISPR CDSs each associated with Cas (CRISPRFinder). My replication finds 31 PGAP-annotated phage/integrase CDSs including a clean structural module (terminase small subunit, portal, major capsid, tail tape measure, integrases), consistent with >=1-2 prophages --- but I cannot count intact regions on the fragmented 420-contig, N50=28kb assembly. MinCED found ZERO CRISPR arrays, which is a known limitation on fragmented assemblies (arrays span contig boundaries). Without a closed or near-closed assembly, both prophage count and CRISPR-Cas type (I-B? II-A? III-A? L. reuteri is known to carry type II-A) remain uncertain.
next_steps: Nanopore-sequence the isolate to >=100x coverage and hybrid-assemble with the existing Illumina MiSeq reads (Unicycler / Trycycler / Flye + polishing).
On the improved assembly, rerun PHASTER (or the FOSS alternative Phigaro / VirSorter2) to get an exact intact/incomplete/questionable prophage count.
Rerun MinCED and CRISPRCasFinder to identify array location(s) and Cas-gene cassette (subtype), then compare with published L. reuteri CRISPR subtypes (typically II-A).
Cross-check whether the assembled CRISPR spacers match phages in the same rumen/gut community (spacer-vs-metagenome, e.g. against the pig-gut virome database).

open_questions.q: Does PNW1 produce a bacteriocin phenotypically active against Shiga-toxigenic E. coli O177, and is the active molecule attributable to the ROV54067.1 'bacteriocin, partial' CDS or to a different gene product?
open_questions.basis: C7 (agar-well-diffusion assay showing 20.0 +/- 1.00 mm crude and 23.3 +/- 1.15 mm partially purified inhibition against STEC O177) is the paper's most translationally interesting claim, but it is wet-lab only and unreachable in silico. The paper attributes the activity to helveticin J (a class-III heat-labile bacteriocin); my PGAP-annotated protein set contains only 'ROV54067.1 bacteriocin, partial' with no subfamily commitment. The linkage between the observed zone-of-inhibition and any specific CDS is not established in the paper --- only inferred from RAST annotation. Given L. reuteri also produces reuterin (a small-molecule antimicrobial from glycerol fermentation, not a peptide), the anti-STEC activity could be reuterin, not a bacteriocin at all.
next_steps: Repeat the agar-well-diffusion assay on the live isolate against STEC O177 with matched controls (heat-inactivated supernatant, protease K-treated supernatant, catalase-treated supernatant, glycerol-supplemented vs -unsupplemented growth).
If activity survives protease K + catalase but is abolished by removing glycerol from the medium, the active molecule is reuterin, not a bacteriocin.
If protease-sensitive, run size-exclusion + activity-guided fractionation and mass-spec to identify the peptide, then match back to a specific PNW1 CDS.
Independently BLAST the ROV54067.1 partial ORF against curated bacteriocin databases (BAGEL4, BACTIBASE) to see whether the closest match is truly a helveticin-family class-III bacteriocin.

open_questions.q: Does PNW1 satisfy the EFSA QPS (Qualified Presumption of Safety) criteria for Limosilactobacillus reuteri as a feed additive, once the genome-based caveats found in this replication are accounted for?
open_questions.basis: The paper's overarching claim is probiotic candidacy for a piglet-gut isolate. L. reuteri (now Limosilactobacillus reuteri) is on the EFSA QPS list, but QPS status carries strain-level qualifications, especially the absence of transferable AMR determinants above resistance-breakpoint MIC. The paper's presence-based AMR screen (only lnuC + tetW) is consistent with QPS if (a) the tet(W) is nonfunctional or the strain MIC is below the EFSA cut-off, and (b) neither locus is on a mobilisable element. Additionally, EFSA QPS for reuteri specifically requires absence of reuterin-mediated cross-toxicity concerns in the target species (piglets). None of this is settled by the paper or by my replication.
next_steps: Generate the EFSA-required MIC panel (tetracycline, lincomycin, plus the standard LAB panel: ampicillin, gentamicin, kanamycin, streptomycin, erythromycin, clindamycin, chloramphenicol, quinupristin-dalfopristin, trimethoprim, ciprofloxacin, rifampicin, vancomycin) using EUCAST/ISO 10932 methodology.

For any MIC above the EFSA reuteri cut-off, whole-genome-search for the responsible determinant and confirm chromosomal (non-mobilisable) location using long-read assembly + oriT / repA / relaxase scan.

Piglet-model tolerance study: single-dose and 28-day repeat-dose safety in weaned piglets, monitoring translocation, biogenic amine production in situ, and reuterin exposure of the intestinal epithelium.
Submit the strain + genome + MIC data to EFSA FEEDAP for a formal QPS strain-qualification opinion; the deposit's 'contaminated' RefSeq flag will need to be resolved before submission.
